Items.Authors: Stephanie S. Guzman, James Hoag, Sarah Gajadhar
Items.Title: Discovering the need for dedicated CMMS support for the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope
Items.Abstract: A CMMS (Computerized Maintenance Management System) is a type of software that helps companies keep track of and organize maintenance work, track and monitor assets, control inventory, document procedures, and generate relevant reporting data.  In 2024, the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope was faced with the task of migrating from a discontinued CMMS platform. During the process of preparing for the migration, inconsistencies among how staff members within different departments use the CMMS became apparent. The Inouye had roughly 30 employees that regularly used the CMMS. This team was made up of technicians, engineers, and supervisors, each of whom had different needs of what they got out of a CMMS. The need for a dedicated employee with experience in software tool configuration and administration to support an accurate and timely migration, maintain consistency of use, work as a liaison between staff and the vendor, and implement new or underutilized features became apparent.

Items.Authors: Jennifer Studer, Devin Crichton, Alexandre Refregier, Keshav Bechoo, H. Cynthia Chiang, Chandrachud B. V. Dash, Sindhu Gaddam, Aditya Krishna Karigiri Madhusudhan, Martin Kunz, Kavilan Moodley, Warren Naidoo, Tasmiya Papiah, Isibabale Qhoboshiyane, Liantsoa F. Randrianjanahary, Benjamin R. B. Saliwanchik, Ajith Sampath, Cornelius Ungerer, Thierry Viant, Anthony Walters
Items.Title: Dish assembly precision for HIRAX
Items.Abstract: The Hydrogen Intensity and Real-time Analysis eXperiment (HIRAX) is a radio interferometer array that is currently being deployed at the South African Radio Astronomy Observatory (SARAO) Square Kilometer Array (SKA) site in South Africa. Its aim is to observe neutral hydrogen (HI) through intensity mapping (IM) in the redshift range of 0.775-2.55. HI IM makes it possible to tomographically probe large, cosmological volumes, enabling constraints on, for example, the dark energy equation of state with its large survey of the southern sky. Systematics are a significant concern in deriving cosmological constraints from HI IM. Instrumental effects therefore need to be carefully controlled and monitored with metrological measurements, in particular the precision of mechanical tolerances in the case of redundant interferometric arrays, such as HIRAX. In this work we present the results and implications of the metrological analysis of the 2025-2026 deployment.

Items.Authors: Miroslav Vulinovic, Pedro Escárate
Items.Title: Documented cases of electromagnetic interference in ground-based optical and infrared observatories
Items.Abstract: Awareness of the detrimental effects of electromagnetic interference (EMI) on radio telescopes has existed for decades. In contrast, optical and infrared observatories have traditionally been considered immune due to the distinct operating principles of their detectors. However, experience has demonstrated that their electronic subsystems, particularly charge-coupled devices (CCD) cameras and infrared detectors readouts, can be vulnerable to EMI. Because CCD cameras and infrared detectors remain at the core of many astronomical instruments, this paper reviews the documented cases of EMI affecting ground-based optical and infrared telescopes. Drawing from more than three decades of technical publications and reports, it identifies recurring EMI sources, coupling mechanisms, and their manifestations in detector performance, along with mitigation strategies and best design practices.

Items.Authors: Juan F. Hernández-Cabrera, Carlos Colodro-Conde, Xana Delpueyo Español
Items.Title: DRAGO-2 spatial stability in orbit: MTF monitoring with lunar and Suez targets
Items.Abstract: DRAGO-2 is a compact short-wave infrared camera operating at 1100 and 1600 nm onboard ALISIO-1, a 6U CubeSat that is the first satellite launched by the Instituto de Astrofísica de Canarias. This work explores the temporal stability of its spatial performance in-orbit using the modulation transfer function (MTF) at Nyquist, MTF_Nyq. Because its ~50 m/px native ground sampling distance impedes the use of standard calibration sites, lunar-limb and slanted-edge Suez Canal imagery is used as an alternative. A common iterative edge-based algorithm is applied to both target classes, which estimates the MTF from the line spread function. The resulting MTF_Nyq values estimated from the images, acquired between October 2025 and June 2026, suggest a plausible degradation of the spatial performance of the camera. Nonetheless, the limited sample size and target-dependent effects complicate definitively quantifying any such phenomenon or pinpointing the underlying physical mechanism.

Items.Authors: Vincenzo Della Corte, Fabio Cozzolino, Giacomo Ruggiero, Andrea Longobardo, Carlo Bettanini, Giacomo Colombatti, Alessio Aboudan, Fabrizio Dirri, Laura Inno, Ivano Bertini, Giuseppe Sindoni
Items.Title: Dust next generation sensor: SiPMi-based instrument for measuring scattered light from dust in extraterrestrial environment
Items.Abstract: Analyzing space dust and icy plumes is essential for understanding planetary environments and potential habitability. The Dust Next Generation Sensor advances this field by combining optical detection with impact sensors to retrieve particle dynamics (mass, velocity, trajectory).A key evolution from Rosetta’s GIADA instrument is the Optical Stage, which employs Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) to detect light scattered by $1\text{--}100\,\mu\text{m}$ grains. Uniquely, this system utilizes SiPMs in "intensity mode" rather than standard photon counting. This generates continuous waveforms where amplitude reflects grain size and pulse width indicates velocity. SiPMs provide superior mechanical robustness and radiation hardness, ensuring precise detection in harsh space environments despite potentially increased dark count rates.

Items.Authors: Lodovico Coccato, Stefano Zampieri, Martino Romaniello, Chiara Spiniello, Wolfram Freudling, Ashley Barnes
Items.Title: EDPS GUI: a modern graphical frontend for the ESO data processing system
Items.Abstract: The ESO Data Processing System (EDPS) is a framework designed to execute data reduction pipelines for ESO’s  instruments at the La Silla Paranal Observatory, and in the future, at the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT).  EDPS supports a wide range of use cases, from online data quality control at the telescope to interactive use. It  has proven to be adequately robust for large-scale processing, and flexible enough to handle different reduction  strategies. EDPS automates the selection of the input files for each reduction recipe of the pipeline, and schedules  their execution according to a selected reduction cascade. The EDPS GUI is a web-based Graphical User Interface  for EDPS designed for scientific and interactive use. It provides a modern, flexible, and user-friendly interface to  run EDPS, including configuring and optimising the creation of datasets, the recipe parameters, and inspecting  the results.

Items.Authors: Gabriel González Rial, José Javier Díaz García, Ricardo Tanausú Génova Santos, Francisco Javier Casas Reinares, Laura Castelló Gomar
Items.Title: Electronics for the LiteBIRD temperature monitoring and control system (TMCS): challenges, progress, and outlook
Items.Abstract: LiteBIRD is a next-generation mission to study the CMB, providing full-sky CMB polarization maps and enabling  constraints on the tensor-to-scalar ratio with unprecedented sensitivity. In addition to its scientific contributions,  the Instituto de Astrof´ısica de Canarias is leading, jointly with the Instituto de F´ısica de Cantabria, the technical  development of the Temperature Monitoring and Compensation System (TMCS) as part of the payload. This  document outlines an initial approach to prototyping temperature monitoring for the 300-mK, 1.8-K, and 4.8-K  stages. It also addresses the requirements imposed on the various temperature ranges involved in the TMCS,  and provides a preliminary analysis of the noise generated by the electronics integrated at prototyping level and  its impact on these requirements.

Items.Authors: Christophe Moins, Dan Popovic, Mario Kiekebusch, Jose Antonio Abad, Constanza Araujo, Helen Bedigan, Martin Brinkmann, Elsa Calmette, Greidy Castellanos, Angela Cortes, Byron Engler, Christoph Frank, Fernando Gago, Elizabeth George, Thomas Grudzien, Ivan Guidolin, Andreas Haimerl, Peter Hammersley, Marcus Haug, Stefan Huber, Paul Jolley, Aglaé Kellerer, Jean-Paul Kirchbauer, Barbara Klein, David Kosten, Johannes Kolmeder, Johan Kosmalski, Paolo La Penna, Ulrich Lampater, Serban Leveratto, Steffan Lewis, Christopher Mandla, Enrico Marchetti, Leander Mehrgan, Jérôme Paufique, Lorenzo Pettazzi, Oliver Pfuhl, Thomas Pfrommer, Malte Scherbarth, Sébastien Tordo, Pablo Zuluaga-Ramírez, Sara Zuccon
Items.Title: ELT phasing and diagnostic system (PDS) control software overview
Items.Abstract: The Phasing and Diagnostic Station (PDS) will host five visible and infrared cameras and their optomechanical components. It will be operated by control software based on the ICS framework (IFW).       The software comprises the following components: Observation Coordination System (OCS), Function Control System (FCS) to control and monitor hardware functions and sensing systems, Detector Control System (DCS) to manage the various wavefront sensor camera systems, Cryostat to maintain the infrared detector at low temperature, using the Cryogenic Control Systems software toolkit.       Control and engineering GUIs, along with templates executed through the IFW sequencer, will send commands to the system via standard interfaces.

Items.Authors: S. Massahi, D. Paredes-Sanz, M. Masteghin, S. Svendsen, D. D. M. Ferreira, A. 'S Jegers, D. Skroblin, L. Cibik, R. Fechner, C. Gollwitzer, M. Krumrey, F. E. Christensen
Items.Title: Enabling next-generation multilayer technology for high-energy x-ray telescopes
Items.Abstract: NiCu/SiNₓ multilayers deposited by reactive magnetron sputtering from a novel split NiCu target are demonstrated as a viable route to broadband hard X-ray telescope optics beyond the 79 keV NuSTAR limit. The split target, equal areas of pure Ni and pure Cu, enables alloy co-sputtering without a pre-alloyed target, yielding amorphous, smooth films with interfacial roughness of 0.51–0.53 nm independent of thickness. A critical NiCu layer threshold of ~2.5 nm is identified, below which interface width rises to 0.75 nm. Four power-law depth-graded stacks (200 and 205 periods) were characterized by XRR at 8.048 keV and synchrotron reflectometry (3.4–10 keV, BESSY II). HAADF-STEM confirms well-ordered bilayers across the full ~1.2 µm depth (σ = 0.35–0.70 nm); EDS reveals ~69 at.% Cu / 31 at.% Ni from differential sputtering yields. Simulated reflectance exceeds 95% to ~55–75 keV, with interference fringes visible to 200 keV.

Items.Authors: Lukas Delaye, Iva Laginja, Pierre Baudoz, Axel Potier, Johan Mazoyer, Raphaël Galicher, Susan F. Redmond, Alexis Lau, A. J. Eldorado Riggs, Dan Sirbu, Emiel H. Por, Rémi Soummer, Laurent Pueyo
Items.Title: Enhanced wavefront sensing for the Roman Coronagraph Instrument: Gaussian probes and compact model validation
Items.Abstract: The Coronagraph Instrument on the Roman Space Telescope will be the first space-based system to demonstrate  closed-loop focal-plane wavefront sensing and control, a key step towards the Habitable Worlds Observatory.  Beyond the baseline Hybrid Lyot Coronagraph, “enhanced modes” are being developed to improve efficiency  and science yield. One such mode uses Gaussian probes for electric field estimation, extending the linear regime  and allowing higher probe amplitudes. This may increase signal-to-noise, reduce exposure time, accelerate  dark hole convergence, and extend operation to stars as faint as V ∼ 5. For those reasons, it was selected  by the Coronagraph Community Participation Program’s Hardware Working Group as the first technology  demonstration carried out on Roman in early 2027. We present numerical simulations using a noise-free compact  software model, which demonstrate the benefits of replacing the nominal probes with Gaussian probes.

Items.Authors: Kevin Phan, J. Zachary Gazak
Items.Title: Enhancing sparse-field astrometry via photometric rank consistency in quad matching
Items.Abstract: Narrow-field telescopes often detect too few stars for reliable catalog matching, making astrometric plate solving ambiguous. We introduce a photometric consistency check that augments the Bayesian log-odds score produced by astrometry.net (Lang et al. 2010) for each candidate quad match. After geometric verification, the four quad stars are cross-matched to the SSTRC7 catalog via the recovered WCS, and Kendall's rank correlation (τ) is computed between observed flux and catalog magnitude. The score is added as a Bayes factor, ℓ_enh = ℓ_raw + ατ, enabling correct near-miss candidates to cross the acceptance threshold. Evaluated in a fully lost-in-space setting on 685 simulated fields (0.25 deg FOV, 512x512 px), at alpha = 15 the method raises normalized AUC of the solve-rate curve from 0.711 to 0.801 (+0.090) over n = 4-20 stars, with peak gains of +47.3 pp (n = 7) and +37.2 pp (n = 6).

Items.Authors: Daniel R. Wilkins, Artem Poliszczuk, Abigail Y. Pan, Leonid Sajkov, Steven W. Allen, Matthew Heine, Catherine E. Grant, Marshall W. Bautz, Tanmoy Chattopadhyay, Kevan Donlon, Sven C. Herrmann, Beverly LaMarr, Eric D. Miller, Peter Orel
Items.Title: Enhancing the sensitivity of next-generation x-ray imaging detectors with artificial intelligence and advanced event reconstruction algorithms
Items.Abstract: Advanced algorithms incorporating artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) enhance the sensitivity of X-ray imaging detectors and the scientific capabilities of future X-ray missions. We report on the development of prototype algorithms designed to provide improved identification of particle-induced background events and enhanced energy reconstruction. ML algorithms can achieve a reduction of the unrejected particle background by up to 60% compared with traditional filtering methods. Moreover, with physics-motivated models of charge diffusion within the device, we find that next-generation event reconstruction algorithms can provide an improvement in the energy resolution of CCD-like detectors at event energies below 0.5keV. We present new laboratory data that demonstrates the performance of these algorithms on next-generation SiSeRO CCD devices. Together such detector and algorithm combinations can satisfy the requirements for future X-ray flagship missions.

Items.Authors: Emily Farr, Nicholas Kruczek, Kevin France, Paloma López Reyes, Juan Larruquert, John Hennessy
Items.Title: Environmental stability testing of narrowband optical coatings in the Lyman-ultraviolet: from the lab to rockets to HWO
Items.Abstract: NASA has prioritized developing optical coatings for the Lyman- and far-ultraviolet (90–200 nm) to support future missions. To advance UV optics for the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO), we present the latest performance measurements and environmental stability results for band-selecting filters designed for the Lyman-ultraviolet bandpass (LUV; 90–120 nm). Lyman-UV coatings can degrade during storage and integration, with humidity reducing the reflectivity of lithium-fluoride overcoated mirrors. The narrowband filters developed with the Grupo de Óptica de Láminas Delgadas (GOLD) are Lyman-α (121.6 nm) suppressing filters peaking near 105 nm (“F110M”), now being flight-tested on the FLUID sounding rocket. We present recent CU Boulder results comparing MgF₂ and AlF₃ capped and uncapped witness samples over the first year of environmental testing, and new results using a liquid polymer protective layer on LiF-overcoated samples.

Items.Authors: Windell Tanaka, Milan Štubljar, Erin Suzuki
Items.Title: ERIN: a radio-quiet autonomous daytime star camera with adaptive background subtraction for stratospheric balloon missions
Items.Abstract: The Payload for Ultrahigh Energy Observations (PUEO) is an Antarctic long-duration balloon experiment designed to search for radio signals from ultrahigh-energy neutrinos and cosmic rays. The Equatorial Reference Imager for Navigation (ERIN) was developed as an autonomous daytime star-camera subsystem for PUEO. This paper presents ERIN’s development and ground-based validation, including localized background subtraction, robust source detection, autoexposure and autogain control, autofocus, star-pattern solving, and attitude estimation. Laboratory, environmental, and on-sky results characterize solution accuracy. Two ERIN instruments were integrated and flown aboard PUEO.

Items.Authors: M. Cecconi, F. Ambrosino, F. Leone, A. Ghedina, F. Dazzi, M. Gonzalez, M. Lodi, M. Hernandez, L. Riverol, J. San Juan, H. Ventura
Items.Title: e-SiFAP: a new enhanced VIS-IR ultrafast photometer at the Telescopio Nazionale Galileo
Items.Abstract: A new, complex and challenging fast photo(VIS-IR)polarimeter(VIS) has been designed for observing compact galactic and extragalactic sources, such as neutron stars and black holes, allowing for detecting sub-second variations in pulsars and gamma-ray bursts. It has been mounted and aligned on optical table in an optical laboratory of the Astronomical Observatory of Rome, ready to be delivered to the optical laboratory of the Fundación Galileo Galilei-INAF in La Palma (Canary Islands) where it will be integrated/aligned on a special optical table which be interfaced with the Telescopio Nazionale Galileo for its final alignment and first light.

Items.Authors: Marlène de Sepibus, Elena Masciadri, Camilo Weinberger, Steffen Mieske, Angel Otarola, Joseph Shields, Christian Veillet
Items.Title: Establishing baseline models' performances for optical turbulence forecasting
Items.Abstract: Accurate forecasting of optical turbulence helps telescopes observe with maximum efficiency as performance of AO systems depends on turbulence conditions. A wide range of forecasting methods has been explored in the literature, varying in complexity, cost, and performance. To appreciate their added value, it is necessary to benchmark them against simple reference models, or baselines, that act as thresholds. In this contribution we present two such baselines and analyze their results for all main astroclimatic and atmospheric parameters at the VLT and LBT. Each method is useful for a specific typology of forecast: prevision by persistence (PP) when we forecast the temporal evolution of a parameter, and precasting (PC) when we forecast the average value of the parameter. Finally, we discuss encouraging preliminary results on estimating these thresholds for sites different from those analysed in this paper.

Items.Authors: Takaki Nakagawa, Naoto Iida, Hiroyuki Hori, Eiji Suzuki, Takeo Manome, Kiichi Kitanaka, Kentaro Yanagibashi, Kazumi Nishikawa, Masatsugu Kamiura, Daisuke Yamanaka, Yuji Ikeda, Hitoshi Tokoro, Taiki Bessho, Masahito S. Uchiyama, Sayumi Kaji, Yoshihiko Saito, Hideaki Kotake
Items.Title: Evaluation of diffraction-limited performance of a large optical antenna for cislunar optical communication system
Items.Abstract: Future Earth–Moon optical communication requires a telescope that can maintain diffraction-limited performance despite severe thermal fluctuations, radiation, and launch loads. Fine Cordierite®, developed by Kyocera, offers ultra-low CTE, high stiffness, radiation resistance, and machinability for complex structures, enabling monolithic and highly athermal optical systems. However, large monolithic telescopes made entirely of this brittle ceramic had not been realized due to the difficulty of assembling precision optical and structural components. Leveraging two decades of accumulated manufacturing and assembly expertise, Kyocera has successfully developed the first all–Fine Cordierite® telescope. This paper summarizes its design, fabrication, and optical performance.

Items.Authors: Éric M. M. Thiébaut, Olivier Flasseur, Samuel Thé, Loïc Denis
Items.Title: Exo-planet detection with ASAP-DC
Items.Abstract: In this contribution, we propose to use the ASAP family of covariance models to take into account the statistics of the residual star light and of the noise in sequences of high-contrast images. In particular, the so-called "hierarchical" ASAP model seems very well suited to account for long-range correlations in the stellar leakages. We developed a fast unsupervised algorithm to learn the ASAP model given the sequence of scientific images and to compute detection maps. Based on ROC curves, taking into account long-range correlations improve the achieved detection contrast notably near the coronagraphic mask, that is close to the host star.

Items.Authors: Antonin Besse, Imran Khan, Alexandra Mazzoli, Colin Dandumont, Jasper Bouwmeester, Denis Defrère, Romain Laugier, Vincent Moreau, Pierre Piron, Rudolf Saathof, Ida Sigusch, Guilhem Terrassa, Pascal Hallibert, David Alaluf, Luca Schifano, Theresa Rank-Lueftinger, Luis Venancio, Nandini Bhattacharya, Jérôme Loicq
Items.Title: Exoplanet Explorer: polarization aberrations in nulling interferometry
Items.Abstract: One of the objectives of modern astronomy is the characterization of terrestrial exoplanets orbiting Sun-like stars in the mid-infrared, where instruments face requirements that can only be overcome by nulling interferometry. However, optical effects such as polarization aberrations require careful attention for they deteriorate the null depth. Using the optical design of the Exoplanet Explorer concept study, we analyze the influence of polarization aberrations over the 3–20 μm band for multiple optical coatings, and, in addition, we describe multiple polarization aberrations compensation strategies and show their impact on the null depth. We present our nulling interferometry testbench, where we experimentally investigate polarization aberrations in the beam combiner and phase shifter to provide more insights into the required polarization considerations. These results will be used to implement polarization control subsystems in our 4 beams broadband nulling interferometry testbench.

Items.Authors: G. Capobianco, V. Noce, D. Loreggia, M. Pancrazzi, S. Fineschi, V. Caracci, D. Bonino, G. Franchi
Items.Title: Expected performances of x and gamma rays detectors being operated on the Moon and in the Earth stratosphere
Items.Abstract: As part of the “Earth Moon Mars (EMM)”project, led by INAF (Istituto Nazionale di Astrofisica) in partnership with ASI (Agenzia Spaziale Italiana) and CNR (Consiglio Nazionale delle Ricerche) and funded under the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (NRRP), we developed the Solar X Ray Moonitor (SXRM), a Moon-based instrument to monitor solar activity from the lunar surface in the energy range of 1 to 30 keV. SXRM has two main objectives: to provide alerts in case of solar storms (flares, CME) directed at the Moon –an essential feature for future permanent missions - and to deliver diagnostics about the parent events. The final delivery of the instrument is currently expected by spring of 2026 at a Technology Readiness Level (TRL) of 4. We have drafted the SXRM engineering and development plan aiming at realizing a space-qualified instrument.This presentation will focus on detector simulations, radiometric computations and the identification of the critical parameters.

Items.Authors: Ricardo Ortiz
Items.Title: Extending aluminum coating life: in situ wet washing results for the 2016 MMT 6.5m primary mirror
Items.Abstract: Wet washing the 2016 coating of the 6.5m MMT primary mirror in-situ has yielded the most recent results. By performing mirror washing once or twice a year, we’ve exceeded the expected lifespan of our coating. We’ll present a comprehensive overview of our 2016 unprotected aluminum coating. Over the years, we’ve maintained the standard aluminum coating on the MMT, on-glass mirrors, using water, soap, and cotton swabs. This approach has preserved the coating properties close to near-fresh levels without causing any visible scratches on the bare aluminum surface. We’ll share data on the lifespan of the 2016 coating using our Konica Minolta Spectrophotometer CM-600d.

Items.Authors: Yuichi Matsuda, Toshihiro Tsuzuki, Naoki Kohara, Kazuhisa Mitsuda, Atsushi Noda, Yuichiro Ezoe, Naoshi Murakami, Satoshi Kikuta
Items.Title: Extremely large optical infrared space telescope with multiple diffractive optical elements
Items.Abstract: We present a concept study of an extremely large optical–infrared space telescope enabled by formation-flying ultra-small satellites. The primary science objective is to spatially resolve surface features of nearby exoplanets with potentially habitable environments. Achieving a spatial resolution of at least 1 micro-arcsecond would allow discrimination of features such as oceans, lands, vegetation, and volcanic activity on exoplanets at a distance of 10 parsecs, corresponding to an effective aperture diameter exceeding 100 km. To realize such a system, we propose a new telescope concept combining electromagnetic formation flying (EMFF) and multiple diffractive optical elements (DOEs). In this study, we investigate the feasibility of this concept, focusing on the application of diffractive optics.

Items.Authors: Mary Iskakova, Kenneth Buffo, Casey DeRoo, Manel Errando, Gavin Frueh
Items.Title: Fabrication and characterization of electroactive polymer actuators for high-resolution adjustable X-ray optics
Items.Abstract: This work explores adjustable X-ray mirror technologies that use electroactive polymer films as actuators to correct figure errors in sub-millimeter-thick mirror segments. Such figure deviations can arise from fabrication defects, mounting stresses, or coating-induced strain and ultimately reduce angular resolution of the optics. We focus on the fabrication, characterization, and application of individually addressable actuator cells based on PVDF-TrFE electroactive polymer films deposited on flat silicon wafers. Electroactive polymers can deliver significant strains at low operating voltages, making them promising for correcting deformations in thin mirror shells of future X-ray telescopes.  We will present an updated fabrication procedure and associated figure changes. We have also developed strategies to identify and recover shorted cells, which we will discuss here.

Items.Authors: Jay Kueny, Joseph D. Long, Jared Males, Alycia Weinberger, Laird Close, Joshua Liberman, Sebastiaan Haffert, Eden McEwen, Maggie Kautz, Jialin Li, Warren Foster, Logan Pearce, Parker T. Johnson, Katie Twitchell, Olivier Guyon, Avalon Gower, Elena Tonucci, Matthijs Mars, Lauren Schatz, Miles Lucas
Items.Title: ffortissimo: a freeform forward-modeling pipeline for high-contrast images of circumstellar disks based on Autodiff/JAX
Items.Abstract: We introduce our efforts towards a data-driven approach for characterizing circumstellar disks with the novel, pixel-based freeform forward modeling pipeline, ffortissimo. We developed ffortissimo within the framework of JAX, which is a machine learning library in Python that enables efficient optimization through automatic differentiation ("autodiff") and GPU-accelerated array computations. Using on-sky visible light images of the disk around HR 4796 taken by the Magellan "extreme" Adaptive Optics instrument (MagAO-X), we demonstrate that our freeform models excel at fitting a complex dust distribution and can infer the dust scattering properties even through PSF subtraction artifacts. We will also exhibit inject and recovery trials showing evidence that ffortissimo can infer morphological features finer than a resolution element. Finally, we will explain the remaining challenges surrounding better noise characterization to improve our model fits.

Items.Authors: Pierre Royer, Leonardo Peri, Wim De Munter, Gert Raskin, Julien Storm, Bart Vandenbussche, Tjorven Delabie, Camille Pirat, Maddalena Reggiani, Hugues Sana, Mikel Samson, Louis Storm, Dirk Vandepitte, Sibo Van Gool, Rhimas Van de Putte, Bram Vandoren, Dominic Bowman
Items.Title: Fine-guidance sensor image simulation and pointing performance assessment for the CubeSpec mission
Items.Abstract: CubeSpec is a 12U CubeSat scheduled for launch in 2027 as an in-orbit demonstrator for high-resolution astrophysical spectroscopy. With a pointing stability expected to be around 1 arcmin, its excellent attitude determination and control system (ADCS) remains to ensure the targets remain focussed in the 2.5 x 6.5 arcsec entrance slit of the spectrograph.    CubeSpec therefore incorporates a secondary pointing subsystem, the High Precision Pointing Platform (HPPP), which employs a closed-loop tip–tilt mirror coupled with a dedicated fine-guidance sensor (FGS). Accurate modelling of the FGS response is essential for predicting the achievable pointing performance.    In this paper, we present an image-simulation tool developed for the FGS, together with a performance assessment of the HPPP. The analysis combines simulated sensor data with hardware test results obtained at both the ADCS and HPPP levels, providing an end-to-end evaluation of the system’s expected on-orbit behaviour.

Items.Authors: Wayne H. Baumgartner, Gianluigi De Geronimo, Jarred M. Roberts, Nabin Poudyal, Wesley Hodge, Valter Bonvicini, Terri Brandt, Sukanya Chakrabarti, Yuri Evangelista, Marco Feroci, Martin Grim, Paul Ray, Eric Wulf, Gianluigi Zampa
Items.Title: First detector results using the new Naval Research Laboratory NSX1 ASIC developed for X-ray coded mask imagers with large area SDDs
Items.Abstract: The NSX1 ASIC is a 64-channel low noise and low power device developed for use with large area silicon X-ray detectors such as the Wide Field Monitor coded mask instrument on the Strobe-X Xray Probe mission concept. The first ASICs were fabricated, delivered and tested in 2025, with early tests showing good ASIC performance of the standalone device, meeting its design goal with a measured noise performance of 5 e- ENC. We report here on the first tests of the ASIC coupled to a Silicon Drift Detector. For these tests we used a single pixel hexagonal SDD 4 mm on a side and 450 um thick connected to one of the ASICs 64 channels.

Items.Authors: Begoña García-Lorenzo, Seifeldin Abouelella, Kabir Baig, Zenaida García Rodríguez, Kshitij Ghimire, Moisés Pulido Torres, Alejandro Trujillo Ramos, Jose A. Acosta-Pulido, Julio A. Castro-Almazán, Donaji Esparza-Arredondo, Antonio Eff-Darwich
Items.Title: Focal-plane diagnostics of atmospheric and dome-induced turbulence: exploring techniques and applications
Items.Abstract: Atmospheric turbulence limits image quality in ground-based astronomy. Its impact depends on the overall turbulence strength, the wavefront spatial-coherence outer scale (L₀), and turbulence generated inside the telescope enclosure. While seeing and related parameters are routinely monitored, measurements of L₀ and dome turbulence remain scarce.  We build on recent methodology for seeing-limited integral-field data to show how spatial information in spectroscopic observations can be used to diagnose these effects. We investigate the feasibility of extending these techniques beyond IFS observations to other seeing-limited instruments through the analysis of wavelength-dependent spatial profiles. We also present the development of data-driven three-dimensional PSF models based on atmospheric statistics for the reconstruction of seeing-limited IFS observations.

Items.Authors: Adam B. Johnson, Christian Marois, Olivier Lardière, William Thompson, Joeleff Fitzsimmons, Dylan Kerr, Andre Fogal, Kaitlyn Hessel, Christoper Mann, Darryl Gamroth, Angus Bews, Scott MacDonald, Alan McConnachie, Tim Hardy, Julien Lozi, Olivier Guyon, Garima Singh, Matthew Wung, Naoyuki Tamura
Items.Title: From Canada to Hawai'i: shipping, commissioning, and practical insights from deploying SPIDERS on the Subaru Telescope
Items.Abstract: We report the logistics for transporting the fully assembled SPIDERS instrument from Canada to Subaru Telescope. This required coordinated scheduling between remote teams, customs and border preparation, and management of controlled goods, lasers, chemicals, and batteries. To protect sensitive hardware and alignment during truck, air, sea, and on-mountain transport, the instrument used wire-rope isolators in a crate designed for controlled lifting and handling. Custom three-axis shock loggers and environmental monitors recorded acceleration, temperature, humidity, and pressure while contamination controls preserved optical cleanliness. Real-time tracking aided response to delays, and secure retention of optics and fasteners limited vibration-induced shifts. These measures enabled rapid unpacking, alignment, and verification on arrival, ensuring that SPIDERS reached Subaru ready for commissioning as a high-contrast imager and spectrograph using focal-plane wavefront sensing behind AO3k.

Items.Authors: Massinissa Hadjara, Hangxin Ji, Qinyang Dong, Marcos Diaz, Mustapha Meftah, Bernard Foing, Zhu Ping
Items.Title: From early concepts to lunar hypertelescopes: roadmap for next-generation optical astronomy on the Moon
Items.Abstract: We present a historical and technical roadmap tracing the evolution of concepts that lead toward future lunar hypertelescopes for ultra-high-resolution optical astronomy. Building on diluted-aperture and interferometric concepts, we exploit recent progress in formation flying, precision metrology and lunar surface operations. The Moon offers unique advantages: seismically quiet ground, no atmosphere, cold traps for cryogenics, and long-term infrastructure potential. These enable sparse to kilometric baseline arrays far beyond Earth-based limits. We review paths from near-term precursor interferometers (10–100 m class) to large hypertelescope networks achieving milli- to micro-arcsecond resolution for direct imaging of exoplanets, stellar surfaces, and compact objects. Key milestones, scientific drivers, and engineering challenges are identified to evolve from current studies toward permanent lunar optical interferometric facilities.

Items.Authors: Massinissa Hadjara, Anton Pomazan, Hangxin Ji, Qinyang Dong, Jinghui Zheng, Yindun Mao, Leonardo Cament, Martin Adams, Marcos Diaz, Rene Mendez, Bernard Foing, Mustapha Meftah, Zhu Ping, Rabah Ikhlef, Djounai Baba-Aissa
Items.Title: From Earth’s harshest landscapes to lunar horizons: engineering telescopes for extreme environments
Items.Abstract: We present a comparative engineering roadmap for optical telescopes designed to operate in extreme environments on Earth and the lunar surface, particularly for investigating small Solar System bodies. Drawing on lessons from high-altitude deserts, polar stations, and remote platforms, we propose solutions for lunar-based telescopes to monitor near-Earth space, increase detectability of near-Earth asteroids (NEAs), and improve follow-up. These telescopes will also observe transient phenomena like gamma-ray bursts, supernovae, and variable stars, while providing data on space weather and radiation. The Moon’s stable platform, lack of atmosphere, and continuous observing windows offer unique advantages for long-term monitoring of NEAs, space debris, and other celestial phenomena. This project outlines engineering concepts for precursor lunar telescopes and discusses milestones for transitioning from Earth-based systems to robust, autonomous lunar implementations for continuous operation.

Items.Authors: David Sanmartim, Alysha Shugart, Anastasia Alexov, Bruno Quint, Eric Christensen, Erik Dennihy, Kevin Fanning, Kshitija Kelkar, Paulina Venegas, Yijung Kang
Items.Title: From issues to insight: a Jira analytics dashboard to prioritize and manage work during NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory commissioning and operations
Items.Abstract: Large observatories accumulate thousands of Jira issues across hardware, software, integration, and procedural work, yet native Jira dashboards remain project-scoped and offer limited support for cross-system triage. We present a lightweight analytics dashboard that turns Jira into an observatory-scale decision-support and triage tool for the Vera C. Rubin Observatory. It converts the unstructured pool of tickets into concise views that highlight where problems cluster, which work is most urgent, and how load is distributed. The paper will describe the dashboard’s architecture and configuration, and provide examples of fault localization, workflow, and workload views used in Rubin commissioning and operations to make triage more efficient and surface bottlenecks earlier. We also outline how other teams can adapt the approach to their own Jira projects by remapping fields and hierarchies, turning the issue tracker into a practical tool for daily operations and backlog governance.

Items.Authors: Alejandro S. Farah Simon, Carolina Keiman, Joel Sanchez-Bermudez, Salvador Cuevas , Fernando Ángeles Uribe, Rubén Flores-Meza, Valente Vázquez, Rebeca García-López, Gerhard Ulbricht
Items.Title: From reverse engineering to manufacturing: finite-element cryogenic and optomechanical validation of the GRAVITY+ SUPER HIGH-RES grism system
Items.Abstract: GRAVITY+ is an upgrade of the VLTI GRAVITY instrument aimed at extending sensitivity to fainter astronomical targets while improving high-contrast performance on bright objects. This contribution presents the reverse-engineering, dimensional verification, and optomechanical validation activities carried out to integrate a new germanium grism into the GRAVITY grism wheel. Finite-element simulations were performed to assess the thermal performance of the optomechanical assembly under cryogenic conditions.

Items.Authors: Elisa Portaluri, Tânia Sofia Gomes Machado, Davide Greggio, Kalyan Kumar Radhakrishnan Santhakumari, Maria Bergomi, Mauro Centrone, Simone Di Filippo, Carmelo Arcidiacono, Alessandro Ballone, Federico Battaini, Oleksandra Rebrysh, Roberto Ragazzoni, Demetrio Magrin, Valentina Viotto, Jacopo Farinato, Gabriele Umbriaco, Gianluca Di Rico, Marco Faccini, Ivan Agostinelli, Michele Frangiamore, Davide Ghiughello, Dhiraj Gupta
Items.Title: From simulations to the telescope: performance assessment of the Ingot WFS
Items.Abstract: The Ingot WFS is a new class of sensor proposed to mitigate the significant geometric differences between Laser (LGSs) and Natural Guide Stars, a challenge amplified in the new generation of extremely large telescopes (ELTs). The I-WFS is designed for an optical system featuring a sufficiently large aperture and a laser launcher located outside the telescope pupil and is specifically conceived and optimized to accommodate the extended nature of LGSs. In this work, we discuss the current state-of-the-art of performance assessment through simulation runs, presenting promising results in terms of incorporating source geometry and reconstructing the atmospheric turbulence. We also outline the path toward our ultimate goal: performing an on-sky validation experiment on a facility configuration reproducing the main characteristics of an ELT. In parallel, we plan the assembly of a portable, standalone system, including the Ingot prism prototype, compatible with the facility interfaces.

Items.Authors: Emaad Paracha, Steven J. Benton, Aurelien A. Fraisse, Ajay S. Gill, John W. Hartley, Bradley Holder, William C. Jones, Lun Li, Thuy Vy T. Luu, Richard J. Massey, Jacqueline E. McCleary, Johanna M. Nagy, C. Barth Netterfield, Susan F. Redmond, Jason D. Rhodes, L. Javier Romualdez, Jurgen Schmoll, Sayan Saha, Bryce Warren, Ben Boyd, Jason Brown, Peter Bartosik, Pablo Trujillo, Philippe Voyer
Items.Title: From sky to screen: improving downlinking over error-prone omni-directional links from the stratosphere
Items.Abstract: Long-duration stratospheric balloon missions must transmit large volumes of scientific and telemetry data over variable, omni-directional links prone to packet loss and bandwidth fluctuations. To address this, we developed a semi-autonomous file-downlink system for high-altitude astronomy missions such as SuperBIT and its successor, GigaBIT. The system comprises a payload client, ground server, and cleaner program capable of operating across UDP and TCP links. The client manages a dynamic queue of data and divides them into fixed-size chunks with metadata, enabling resumable transfers and selective retransmissions. This chunk-level approach ensures only corrupted data is resent, reducing bandwidth usage. The system helps increase overall throughput, substantially improving telemetry downlink in constrained stratospheric telescope missions. This talk presents the system design and protocol behaviour, along with the performance during SuperBIT’s final flight.

Items.Authors: Liana De Filippis, Enrico Cascone
Items.Title: From the stable to the stars: a PNRR-funded concurrent design facility born from a rural ruin
Items.Abstract: This PNRR-funded restoration project has revitalized a historic 18th-century building at the Capodimonte Astronomical Observatory in Naples. Initially housing colonists and later repurposed as an agricultural stable, the derelict structure was an architectural witness to the rural-scientific past of the Miradois hill. The project involved a meticulous philological and functional restoration, guided by archival research, prioritizing the reinstatement of the original morphology while implementing advanced conservative techniques, including structural consolidation and seismic upgrading.The recovered building now houses a cutting-edge Concurrent Design Facility (CDF)—the first in Southern Italy. Dedicated to the collaborative design of complex space and astronomical systems, the CDF connects multidisciplinary teams with major European research centers. The project's deep value lies in the powerful from the stable to the stars metaphor.

Items.Authors: Cihan Tuğrul Tezcan, Onur Şatır, Cahit Yeşilyaprak
Items.Title: Full robotic transformation of the DAG-turbulence profiling station (DAG-TPS) for autonomous atmospheric monitoring
Items.Abstract: The DAG-Turbulence Profiling Station (DAG-TPS) monitors atmospheric turbulence using simultaneous DIMM and MASS-DIMM measurements. Although originally operated remotely, it still required human interaction, limiting continuity and efficiency. This study introduces the full robotic conversion of the system, including autonomous scheduling, environmental-awareness logic, fault-tolerant operation, and hardware upgrades for reliable unattended use. Early tests show major improvements in temporal coverage and data consistency, enabling continuous turbulence characterization at the DAG Observatory and providing a foundation for future adaptive-optics planning.

Items.Authors: M. De Lucia, P. Dal Bo, J. Cliche, S. Della Torre, M. Dobbs, T. Lari, K. Leonova, A. Limonta, M. Massa, A. Moggi, J. Montgomery, D. Nicolò, A. Passerini, M. Pinchera, A. Tartari, G. Smecher, M. Zannoni, G. Signorelli
Items.Title: Functionality and performance of the upgraded design of the LiteBIRD SQUID controller unit in a full read-out chain
Items.Abstract: LiteBIRD is a spaceborne telescope scheduled for launch in the 2030s to measure the polarization anisotropies of the CMB and provide high sensitivity polarization maps with unprecedented frequency coverage. A likely option for the readout chain involves a dual-stage SQUID amplification in order to meet the SNR and the thermal-budget requirements .It uses a front-end SQUID placed close to the detectors to provide a small gain while decoupling the TES bias circuit from the readout impedance. A second SQUID provides the high-gain amplification and can be located on a warmer stage with less constraints on power dissipation.  The new SQUID Controller Unit design addresses the issue of operating two cascaded SQUIDs and has been modified in order to match thermo-mechanical requirements in view of TRL6 qualification. In this work, we report on the ongoing development of the control electronics for the DSS and we show the first end-to-end performance test of the complete readout chain.

Items.Authors: José M. Filgueira, Jordi Molgó, Marianne Cox, Jorge Barrios
Items.Title: GMT integrated adaptive optics RTC design and prototype: new technology challenges and opportunities
Items.Abstract: The next generation of Extreme Large Telescopes (ELTs) will incorporate Adaptive Optics as an integral component of their wavefront control system. In this paper, we present the progress made in designing and implementing a prototype of an Integrated Adaptive Optics Real Time Computer (RTC) for the Giant Magellan Telescope (GMT). We conducted a comprehensive requirements analysis to validate that the prototype is able to achieve the necessary compute throughput, bandwidth (both memory and network), and storage to meet the higher-level end-to-end loop latency and telemetry requirements.

Items.Authors: Sanghyuk Kim, Woojin Park, Chan Park, Sungho Lee, Heeyoung Oh, Moo-Young Chun, Hyun-Jeong Kim, Sang-Mok Cha, Ueejeong Jeong, Gregory N. Mace, Cynthia B. Brooks, Hanshin Lee, John M. Good, Cooper W. Dix, Alycia J. Weinberger, Daniel T. Jaffe
Items.Title: GMTNIRS: mechanical design strategy for the MagNIFIES pathfinder on Magellan Telescope
Items.Abstract: The Giant Magellan Telescope Near-Infrared Spectrograph (GMTNIRS) is a first-generation near-infrared spectrograph for GMT, providing high-resolution (R ≈ 65,000–80,000) spectroscopy over 1.08–5.40 μm. We plan to develop the Magellan Near-IR Five-band Immersion grating Efficient Spectrograph (MagNIFIES) as a natural-seeing pathfinder instrument for the Magellan telescope prior to GMT's completion. MagNIFIES offers the same wavelength coverage but with slightly lower resolving power (R ≈ 45,000-65,000). The two instruments share the optical design for the spectrograph, with differences in foreoptics, slit size, electronics, software, and the telescope interface. Because of the reduced mass limit on the Magellan Nasmyth rotator, we discuss a mechanical design strategy for using the same cryostat while reducing the mass and satisfying the requirements of both instruments. We present the the thermal budget calculations and analysis results for the revised mechanical design.

Items.Authors: Woojin Park, Sanghyuk Kim, Heeyoung Oh, Moo-Young Chun, Hyun-Jeong Kim, Gregory Mace, Ueejeong Jeong, Hanshin Lee, Sungho Lee, Chan Park, John M. Good, Cynthia Brooks, Sang-Mok Cha, Bi-Ho Jang, Alycia J. Weinberger, Cooper W. Dix, Daniel T. Jaffe
Items.Title: GMTNIRS: preliminary mechanical design of pupil rotator for a cryogenic near-infrared spectrograph
Items.Abstract: We present the preliminary mechanical design of a pupil rotator developed for the Giant Magellan Telescope Near-Infrared Spectrograph (GMTNIRS). In the infrared, thermal radiation and scattered light from outside the clear aperture of the telescope primary mirror introduce significant background noise. To mitigate this effect, a mask is placed at the pupil plane. The pupil rotator is a cryogenic mechanism that rotates the mask to track the telescope pupil orientation. The system comprises a pupil mask, worm gear assembly, cryogenic motor, Hall sensor for home positioning, and a gearbox. We report finite element analysis results conducted to calculate spring and flexure preloads and to estimate the operating temperature of the pupil mask. We also introduce a prototype pupil rotator equipped with a warm stepper motor, which is being operated at room temperature prior to cryogenic testing.

Items.Authors: Heeyoung Oh, Sanghyuk Kim, Woojin Park, Moo-Young Chun, Hyun-Jeong Kim, Ueejeong Jeong, Sungho Lee, Chan Park, Jae-Rim Koo, Jae Sok Oh, Sang-Mok Cha, Hyeon Cheol Seong, Bi-Ho Jang, Jae-Joon Lee, Ho-Gyu Lee, Young Sam Yu, Gregory N. Mace, Cynthia B. Brooks, Hanshin Lee, John M. Good, Kyle F. Kaplan, Karina Leppik, Cooper Dix, Alycia J. Weinberger, Daniel T. Jaffe
Items.Title: GMTNIRS: prototyping and test
Items.Abstract: We present the prototyping and experimental activities for the development of the Giant Magellan Telescope Near-Infrared Spectrograph (GMTNIRS). GMTNIRS is an advancement beyond its predecessor, the Immersion Grating Infrared Spectrometer (IGRINS), and its extended wavelength coverage to 5.4 µm makes thermal-radiation control a critical aspect of the design. The operating components of GMTNIRS are seven H2RG detectors, electronics and control systems compliant with GMT requirements through an EtherCAT-based architecture, and a cryogenic pupil rotator. These efforts also support the MagNIFIES project, enabling earlier application of GMTNIRS capabilities on a Magellan Telescope. Comprehensive verification plan matrix has been developed, and a dedicated test chamber has been manufactured to validate key instrument aspects, including thermal control, radiation shielding, and customized detector cabling. This presentation will share the overall prototyping plan and early results.

Items.Authors: Quentin Fournier, Guillaume Bourdarot, Vishaal Gopinath, Frank Eisenhauer, Helmut Feuchtgruber, Dieter Lutz, Etienne Rosin, Stefan Gillessen, Reinhard Genzel, Oliver Pfuhl, Taro Shimizu, Felix Mang, Michael Hartl, Thomas Ott, Ekkehard Wieprecht, Françoise Delplancke-Stroebele, Luis Esteras Otal, Felix Widmann, Sebastiano von Fellenberg, Pierre Bourget, Guy Perrin, Julien Woillez, Paulo Garcia, Sebastian Hönig, Laura Kreidberg, Jean-Baptiste Le Bouquin, Thibaut Paumard, Christian Straubmeier
Items.Title: GRAVITY+: reducing non-common-path aberrations for sub-10μas astrometric accuracy
Items.Abstract: GRAVITY is a state-of-the-art instrument for near-infrared astrometric interferometry that routinely achieves astrometric accuracy of 30-100 μas in its phase-referenced dual-field mode. However, its fundamental limit is not yet reached, and can still be improved by several factors. We focus on the effect of systematics, non-common path aberrations between the science channel and the metrology signal in the GRAVITY Fiber Coupler. We have characterized these high-order wavefront errors with nanometer precision in the laboratory. We characterized on-sky the effect of these high-order wavefront imperfections on narrow-angle astrometry. High-precision mirrors, bringing an order of magnitude improvement over existing GRAVITY injection optics, are currently in production and will be installed in the fiber coupler units by the end of 2027. This upgrade is expected to enable astrometric accuracy at the sub-10 μas level in dual-field mode with integration times of just a few minutes.

Items.Authors: Jules Fowler, Rebecca Jensen-Clem, Sylvain Cetre, Maaike A. M. van Kooten, Maïssa Salama, Antonin Bouchez, Avinash Surendran, Charlotte Guthery, Eduardo Marin, Mahawa Cissé, Max Service, Charlotte Z. Bond, Emiel Por, Nour Skaf, Will Gauvin
Items.Title: Ground control to major time-lag: on-sky results of data-driven predictive wavefront control at Keck Observatory
Items.Abstract: Directly imaging and characterizing exoplanets requires extreme adaptive optics (XAO), to achieve exquisite wavefront correction over a small field of view. Predictive wavefront control (PWFC) mitigates temporal errors (often a leading term in these XAO systems) by predicting where the wavefront will be by the time the system correction is applied. In particular, empirical orthogonal functions (EOF) learn correlations in a wavefront using wavefront sensor history. We present on-sky results of a new implementation of EOF built directly into the Keck-II real time controller (RTC). This work revitalizes previous PWFC work at Keck, by showing improved performance over an integral controller during on-sky observing. Finally, we discuss optimization strategies for EOF on sky. This work not only improves current observing for the Keck community, but also acts as a pathfinder for predictive control methods with extremely large telescopes.

Items.Authors: Mark Mueller, Andrew Szentgyorgyi, Sagi Ben-Ami, Isaac Anderson, Daniel Baldwin, Daniel Durusky, Ofir Hershko, Colby Jurgenson, Kenneth McCracken, Heeyoung Oh, Jae Sok Oh, Cem Onyuksel, William Podgorski, Chan Park, Matthew Smith, Yahel Sofer-Rimalt, Abigail Unger, Joseph Zajac
Items.Title: Hardware fabrication update for the GMT-consortium large earth finder (G-CLEF)
Items.Abstract: The GMT-Consortium Large Earth Finder (G-CLEF) is a fiber-fed, optical echelle spectrograph that will be a first light instrument for the Giant Magellan Telescope (GMT). G-CLEF is a general-purpose echelle spectrograph with precision radial velocity (PRV) capability. We will design and build an interim installation configuration for G-CLEF at Magellan’s 6.5m Clay telescope. This paper provides an update on construction of the instrument. It discusses the fabrication and integration of several completed subsystems including the optical bench, vacuum chamber, major optical subassemblies, the Clay front end, electrical systems, and fixturing.

Items.Authors: Amelia Calderhead, Anna MacIver, David Isherwood, Andy Born, James Stevenson
Items.Title: HARMONI at ELT: developing a modular review process using TRIZ
Items.Abstract: The HARMONI team at UKATC have been pioneering the use of TRIZ by managing monthly TRIZ workshops to tackle significant project problems that arise. This TRIZ case study investigates how design changes of HARMONI can be reviewed effectively and efficiently. It draws on how the review process of Ground Based Astronomy projects can be improved to add quality to the successful creation of an instrument while reducing strain on designers and reviewer’s time.   To address resource-intensive and document-driven review processes, the case study utilised TRIZ techniques including; thinking in time & scale technique: the 40 inventive principles to tackle design contradiction: function analysis and size, time, cost analysis.  The solution developed considered a modular, continuous review process focusing on specific subsystems or technical topics as they mature while encouraging a live review culture, where stakeholders and expert reviewers are engaged continuously through informal check-ins.

Items.Authors: P. Bañares-Palacios, M. A. Cagigas, A. A. Luján González, B. García-Lorenzo, A. Alonso, A. de Lorenzo-Cáceres
Items.Title: HARMONI at ELT: integral field spectrograph pre-optics (IPO) design after rescope process
Items.Abstract: HARMONI is the first light, adaptive optics assisted, near-IR integral field spectrograph for the ELT. It covers a spectral range from 750nm to 2450nm with resolving powers from 3000 to 7000 and spatial sampling of 25mas and 6mas. It can operate in two adaptive optics modes - SCAO (including a high contrast capability) and MCAO. The project is resuming its final design phase after a rescope design phase in 2025.     The instrument faced budgetary constraints that led to a reduction in the number of available scales in the IPO subsystem. An overview of the process and final design is presented, where 4x4mas, 10x10mas, 20x20mas and 60x30mas scales (in addition to the pupil imaging scale for alignment, which was preserved) were substituted by 6x6mas and 25x25mas scales, compromising technical requirements and scientific needs.

Items.Authors: Rafael Melgar Hernandez, Yolanda Martin, Elvio Hernández Suárez, Alejandro Antonio Luján González, Alberto Hernández González, Horacio Rodriguez Delgado, Felix Gracia Témich, Miguel Angel Cágigas García, Ángel Alonso, Adriana de Lorenzo Cáceres, Begoña García Lorenzo
Items.Title: HARMONI at ELT: laboratory tests for optimization and validation of the scale changer turret mechanism
Items.Abstract: HARMONI is the first light, adaptive optics assisted, near-IR integral field spectrograph for the ELT. It covers a spectral range from 800nm to 2450nm with resolving powers from 3000 to 7000 and spatial sampling of 25mas and 6mas. It can operate in two adaptive optics modes - SCAO (including a high contrast capability) and MCAO. The project is resuming its final design phase after a rescope design phase in 2025.    This paper reports on the comprehensive testing campaign of the HARMONI IFS Pre-Optic’s (IPO) Scale Changer Turret (SCT) prototype. The primary aim of these tests was to validate the proposed mechanical solution and confirm the overall system performance. We present a detailed analysis of the system and the laboratory setup.

Items.Authors: Eduard R. Muslimov, Matthias Tecza, Edgar Castillo-Domínguez, James Kariuki, Liam Boland, Miriam Cisneros Gonzalez, Kieran McCall, Sophie Paszynska
Items.Title: HARMONI at ELT: optical design of the spectrograph sub-system
Items.Abstract: HARMONI is an adaptive optics assisted, near-IR integral field spectrograph for the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT). The University of Oxford is in charge of the design and development of the four identical spectrographs that disperse the light and form scientific images. During the instrument rescope phase, we have developed a new spectrograph optical design. It uses a two-mirror unobscured freeform collimator, a set of six volume-phase holographic grisms as the disperser, and a two-mirror unobscured freeform camera. This design is up to 350 mm shorter than the previous version. The number of optical elements' positioning parameters is reduced by more than two times. The expected as-built minimum transmission is 57%, while the scattered light level is decreased.

Items.Authors: Vladislavs Plesanovs, Paolo Soffitta, Hemanth Manikantan, Daniel Saueraland, Klaus Desch, Jochen Kaminski, Carlo Lefevre, Ettore Del Monte
Items.Title: Heavy ion irradiation of GridPix gas detector: a step forward for its use in space
Items.Abstract: The GridPix technology is a candidate to be used as a polarimeter on the potential successor  of IXPE, the EXPO or Enhanced X-ray Polarimetry Observatory. Dedicated set of runs was performed at Bonn Isochronous Cyclotron at HISKP, University of Bonn, to test heavy ion influence in MeV energy range. In a gasseous detector these particles induce overwhelming amount of charge that can saturate the electronics readout or induce sparks and rapidly age the detector. GridPix was subjected to two test beams at a low rate, proton beam at 14MeV and 100MeV 14N5++ ions. The GridPix detector contains the readout ASIC, Timepix, with 256 × 256 pixel grid with a pitch of 55 μm and covered with a protection layer plus gas. The Al grid stands on the SU8 pillars above pixels forming the amplification stage enabling primary electron detection. We describes the setup and results of these tests. The observed impact of irradiation is shown for both types of beam.

Items.Authors: Robert Conwell, Stephen S. Eikenberry, Peter Delfyett, Anish Roshi, Shahebul Hasan, Jiabao Li, Jordan Richey, David Smith, Thuy Nguyen, Amith Debnath, Liam Gallagher
Items.Title: Heliocomb: a laser frequency comb heterodyne spectrometer for R=20,000,000,000 solar observations
Items.Abstract: We demonstrate a near-infrared heterodyne instrument which achieves a signal-to-noise ratio sufficient for Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI). VLBI in the near-infrared, achieved by means of heterodyne systems, has the potential to enable ground-based diffraction-limited resolution of millimeter-sized objects in low Earth orbit. Our instrumental design employs an electro-optically modulated laser frequency comb (LFC) as a single-frequency local oscillator with tunability enabled by a calibrated linear stage. Our design is conducive to an instrument with the long-term stability of a LFC, a tunable local oscillator, and scalability for broad instantaneous bandwidth. To demonstrate the efficacy of our instrument, we perform heterodyne spectroscopy on the Sun to measure the Solar Gravitational Redshift, improve upon the current best measurement, and demonstrate year-timescale instrumental stability. This is an essential first step towards near-infrared VLBI.
